title: Hosea 9:1–9
context: Hosea 9:1–9 is spoken mainly by Hosea, who addresses Israel directly and refers to the LORD as "my God" (9:8). He tells Israel not to rejoice like the nations at harvest, because they have been unfaithful and have loved a prostitute’s wages at the threshing floors, likely a reference to harvest rites linked with Baal worship. The threshing floor and winepress will not feed them; they will not stay in the LORD’s land but will return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria, where they cannot offer acceptable worship. 11:5 speaks differently about Egypt, and the two are named without forcing a single explanation. The days of reckoning have come, and the people call the prophet a fool and the inspired man insane. Hosea says the prophet is a watchman with God, yet a snare is set on his paths. They have corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah (Judges 19–21). Shared ground: both traditions read the unit as a warning that festivals and offerings cannot cover unfaithfulness, and as showing the cost of rejecting God’s messengers.

verses.text: Don’t rejoice, Israel, to jubilation like the nations; for you were unfaithful to your God. You love the wages of a prostitute at every grain threshing floor.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea tells Israel not to rejoice like the nations, for they have been unfaithful and loved a prostitute’s wages at every threshing floor. Arminian readers see harvest joy turned into a warning, since the people credited their harvest to Baal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the imagery soberly, as a picture of spiritual unfaithfulness tied to harvest worship. Both traditions note that Hosea uses marriage language to describe covenant betrayal throughout the book.

verses.text: The threshing floor and the wine press won’t feed them, and the new wine will fail her.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says the threshing floor and winepress will not feed them, and the new wine will fail. Arminians see the loss of the very harvest the people thought Baal provided.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God showing that he alone gives grain and wine (compare 2:8). Both traditions read the verse as covenant judgment that exposes the futility of false worship.

verses.text: They won’t dwell in the LORD’s land; but Ephraim will return to Egypt, and they will eat unclean food in Assyria.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says they will not dwell in the LORD’s land, but Ephraim will return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria. Arminian readers see exile as the loss of the land God gave them, which was a sign of covenant blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the return to Egypt as a reversal of the exodus. Both traditions read Egypt here as a figure for bondage, alongside the literal exile to Assyria. They note that 11:5 speaks differently about Egypt, naming the verses without forcing a single explanation.

verses.text: They won’t pour out wine offerings to the LORD, neither will they be pleasing to him. Their sacrifices will be to them like the bread of mourners; all who eat of it will be polluted; for their bread will be for their appetite. It will not come into the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says they will not pour wine offerings to the LORD, and their sacrifices will be like mourners’ bread, defiling all who eat it. Arminians see exile ending acceptable worship, since sacrifices could not be offered in a foreign land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as showing the loss of access to God’s house. Both traditions note that food touched by mourning was considered unclean (compare Numbers 19:14 and Deuteronomy 26:14).

verses.text: What will you do in the day of solemn assembly, and in the day of the feast of the LORD?
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea asks what they will do on the day of solemn assembly and the feast of the LORD. Arminian readers see a sorrowful question, since in exile the people would have no way to celebrate God’s appointed festivals.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the question as highlighting what Israel would lose. Both traditions read it as a call to reflect on the cost of unfaithfulness.

verses.text: For, behold, when they flee destruction, Egypt will gather them up. Memphis will bury them. Nettles will possess their pleasant things of silver. Thorns will be in their tents.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says that when they flee destruction, Egypt will gather them, Memphis will bury them, and thorns will fill their tents. Arminians see a picture of dying in a foreign land, far from the inheritance God gave.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image of abandoned homes overgrown with thorns. Both traditions note that Memphis was a major Egyptian city known for its tombs, and they read the verse as describing exile and death.

verses.text: The days of visitation have come. The days of reckoning have come. Israel will consider the prophet to be a fool, and the man who is inspired to be insane, because of the abundance of your sins, and because your hostility is great.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says the days of reckoning have come, and Israel calls the prophet a fool and the inspired man insane because of its great sin. Arminian readers see the people rejecting God’s messengers, which shows how deep their rebellion had become.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the hardening that comes with persistent sin. Both traditions note that some read the second part as the people’s mocking words and others as Hosea’s description, and they hold the question open.

verses.text: A prophet watches over Ephraim with my God. A fowler’s snare is on all of his paths, and hostility in the house of his God.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says the prophet is a watchman over Ephraim with his God, yet a snare is on his paths and hostility in God’s house. Arminians see the prophet’s faithful role opposed by those he was sent to warn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the watchman image as describing the prophet’s calling (compare Ezekiel 3:17). Both traditions note that the verse is difficult in Hebrew and read in more than one way, and they hold the details loosely.

verses.text: They have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah. He will remember their iniquity. He will punish them for their sins.
verses.arminianNotes: Hosea says they have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah, and God will remember their iniquity. Arminian readers see Israel’s sin compared to one of the darkest episodes in its history (Judges 19–21).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the comparison as showing the depth of Israel’s corruption. Both traditions read the reference soberly and note that Gibeah appears again in 10:9.
